title: Poland's regions · GeoClick Geography
edition: Regions of Europe · one lesson per country · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Poland's regions, part 1 of 1. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
We work through 16 of the Poland regions the map names, once each: where it sits, one fact worth keeping, and a hook to remember it by.

states.name: Pomorskie
lines: Pomorskie runs along the Baltic coast in Poland’s north, with Gdańsk as its largest city, between Zachodniopomorskie in the west and Warmińsko-Mazurskie in the east.
Its name means “along the sea” and shares its root with the German Pommern next door, and Gdańsk was a free city between the wars before its shipyard gave Solidarity its name in August 1980.
Remember the finger of the Hel peninsula reaching 35 kilometres into the Baltic on a spit barely 300 metres wide, and the shipyard gate where the strikes began.

states.name: Warmińsko-Mazurskie
lines: Warmińsko-Mazurskie lies inland in Poland’s north-east, with Olsztyn as its largest city, between Pomorskie on the Baltic coast to the west and Podlaskie in the east.
The name pairs two peoples, the Varmians and the Masurians, and this is the land of a thousand lakes, the last corner of Poland where Old Prussian was still spoken into the 1700s.
Remember the two tribes in one hyphen, the lakes between them, and the Elbląg canal that lifts boats onto rail cradles and carries them overland.

states.name: Zachodniopomorskie
lines: Zachodniopomorskie fills Poland’s north-west, on the Baltic and hard against Germany, with Szczecin as its largest city.
Its name is the western half of “along the sea”, and Szczecin was German until 1945, a city that is older than the Polish state itself.
Remember the western along-the-sea, and the island town of Świnoujście, the only Polish town spread over more than forty islands.

states.name: Podlaskie
lines: Podlaskie sits in Poland’s far north-east, with Białystok as its largest city, between Mazowieckie in the centre and Warmińsko-Mazurskie to the north-west.
The name probably means “under the forest”, and Białowieża here holds one of the last primeval lowland forests in Europe and the largest herd of wild European bison.
Remember the forest under the name, and the wooden Tatar mosques from the 1700s, settled by cavalry soldiers who were given land for their service.

states.name: Kujawsko-Pomorskie
lines: Kujawsko-Pomorskie lies in north-central Poland, inland behind the Baltic coast, with Bydgoszcz as its largest city and five other regions meeting around it.
The name joins two landscapes, the bare windy ground of Kujawy and the sea-coast Pomorze, and Toruń here is where Copernicus was born.
Remember the region of two halves, and the salt graduation towers of Ciechocinek, where brine drips through blackthorn twigs and the air itself has been breathed as a cure since 1824.

states.name: Wielkopolskie
lines: Wielkopolskie spreads across Poland’s west-central plains, with Poznań as its largest city, and it touches seven other regions.
Greater Poland is greater because it is older, the first Polish state around Gniezno and Poznań in the 900s, and Gniezno became Poland’s first archbishopric in the year 1000.
Remember the older Poland, where every early king was crowned at Gniezno before Kraków took over, and which gave Małopolska its name as the younger land.

states.name: Lubuskie
lines: Lubuskie lies in Poland’s far west along the Oder, with Zielona Góra as its largest city and Germany beyond the river.
The region was created in 1999 and named after Lubusz, a town that lies on the German side of the Oder, so it carries the name of a place it does not contain.
Remember the most wooded region in Poland, whose unfinished German bunkers around Międzyrzecz now shelter the largest bat colony in Europe.

states.name: Mazowieckie
lines: Mazowieckie spreads across the centre-east of Poland, with Warsaw as its largest city and the capital of the whole country, ringed by six other regions.
The name comes from the Mazovians, a Polish tribe, and Warsaw was only a Mazovian town until the king moved the court there from Kraków in 1596.
Remember the birthplace of Chopin at Żelazowa Wola, and the 85 per cent of Warsaw deliberately destroyed in 1944, then rebuilt from paintings of the city that no longer existed.

states.name: Łódzkie
lines: Łódzkie lies in the centre of Poland, with the city of Łódź as its largest city and six regions meeting around it.
The name means “boat” and the city’s coat of arms shows one, though it stands on no navigable river, and Piotrkowska Street runs straight for over four kilometres.
Remember the boat on the coat of arms, and the textile city laid out like Manchester, which grew from 800 people to 300,000 in a single century.

states.name: Lubelskie
lines: Lubelskie lies in Poland’s east, with Lublin as its largest city, between Mazowieckie in the centre and Podlaskie in the north-east.
The Union of Lublin was signed here in 1569, joining Poland and Lithuania into one commonwealth that lasted two hundred years.
Remember the ideal Renaissance town of Zamość, built complete in the 1580s and still standing exactly as it was first drawn.

states.name: Dolnośląskie
lines: Dolnośląskie fills Poland’s south-west, with Wrocław as its largest city, between Lubuskie in the west and the Czech border to the south.
Lower Silesia takes its name from the Ślęża mountain and the tribe that lived below it, and Wrocław has been Polish, Bohemian, Austrian, Prussian and German before returning in 1945.
Remember the region with more castles than any other in Poland, and Wrocław’s centenary hall, the first great reinforced concrete dome.

states.name: Świętokrzyskie
lines: Świętokrzyskie lies in south-central Poland, with Kielce as its largest city and the low Holy Cross mountains standing in the middle of it.
It is named for the abbey on Łysa Góra that claimed a relic of the True Cross, and its mountains are among the oldest in Europe, worn down to gentle ridges long before the Alps existed.
Remember the oldest mountains in Poland, low and worn smooth, and the flint mines of Krzemionki that were worked 5,000 years ago.

states.name: Opolskie
lines: Opolskie is the smallest region in Poland, lying in the south with Opole as its largest city, wedged between Dolnośląskie in the west and Śląskie in the east.
Its name comes from Opole, which in Old Slavic meant a community of villages holding land together, and the region has Poland’s largest German minority, so the road signs here are bilingual.
Remember the small region whose name means the group of villages, where the signposts read in two languages and the villages keep winning the best-kept village competitions.

states.name: Śląskie
lines: Śląskie occupies Poland’s far south-west, around Katowice as its largest city, on the border with Czechia and Slovakia.
It is Silesia without a qualifier, the upper part where the coal lies, and it is the most densely populated region in the country.
Remember the crowded coal country, where whole districts were built for miners and the rail network is the densest in Poland.

states.name: Podkarpackie
lines: Podkarpackie fills Poland’s south-east under the Carpathians, with Rzeszów as its largest city and Ukraine close along its eastern edge.
The name means “under the Carpathians”, and the region is one of the poorest in Poland as well as the most forested after Lubuskie.
Remember the oil wells dug by hand at Bóbrka in 1854, older by five years than the Drake well in Pennsylvania that began the American oil rush.

states.name: Małopolskie
lines: Małopolskie fills Poland’s south, with Kraków as its largest city, between Świętokrzyskie in the north and Śląskie in the west, with the Carpathian hills along its southern edge.

Lesser Poland means the younger land, added after Greater Poland, and Kraków was the capital for five centuries, keeping the royal castle, the university and the coronation cathedral after the court left.
Remember the salt mine at Wieliczka, worked since the 1200s, with its chapels and chandeliers carved entirely from rock salt.

recap: 16 regions of Poland, one for each target of the map: Pomorskie, Warmińsko-Mazurskie, Zachodniopomorskie, Podlaskie, Kujawsko-Pomorskie, Wielkopolskie, Lubuskie, Mazowieckie, Łódzkie, Lubelskie, Dolnośląskie, Świętokrzyskie, Opolskie, Śląskie, Podkarpackie and Małopolskie.
Remember the shape of Poland from the inside: the regions nest around each other, and every name on the map belongs somewhere in this one country.
